UC IPM — Olive Herbicide Treatment Table (University of California Integrated Pest Management Program)
source.note: Olive oil — glyphosate kg_ha: Directed post-emergence application for weed control in established olive orchards. UC IPM registered rate 0.8–1.5 lb a.e./acre for in-season applications; midpoint 1.15 lb/acre = 1.29 kg/ha per application. Conventional Mediterranean systems apply 1–2 times annually under-canopy or as strip treatment; global weighted average ~1.0 kg a.i./ha/yr. Glyphosate is the dominant herbicide in Spanish olive production (>90% of no-till orchards) and is widely used in California, Tunisia, and other producing regions.

source.title: USDA NASS — Agricultural Chemical Use Survey
source.note: Olive oil — glyphosate kg_ha: USDA NASS Fruits survey data for California olive orchards corroborates UC IPM registered rate; glyphosate is the most frequently applied herbicide in US olive production. Application rates consistent with 1.0–1.5 kg a.i./ha/yr for conventional systems applying 1–2 directed sprays annually for weed suppression under trees.

source.title: UC IPM — Olive Herbicide Treatment Table (University of California Integrated Pest Management Program)
source.note: Olive oil — pendimethalin kg_ha: Pre-emergence herbicide applied at 1.9–3.8 lb a.i./acre (Prowl H2O) in California olive orchards; full-field rate 3.19 kg/ha. Applied as directed strip treatment to ~50% of orchard floor in many operations, yielding an effective ~0.5–1.0 kg a.i./ha on a whole-orchard area basis. Not used in all Mediterranean systems; more prevalent in intensively managed California and newer Spanish super-intensive orchards. Value of 0.5 kg/ha reflects typical use in the fraction of global olive production where this herbicide is registered and applied.

source.title: Lozano et al. (2021) — Pesticide Residues in Honeybees, Bumblebees and Olive Oil after Applications Against Olive Fruit Fly (PMC/Insects)
source.note: Olive oil — imidacloprid kg_ha: Neonicotinoid insecticide used for olive fruit fly (Bactrocera oleae) control and other sucking pests. Applied as bait spray at field trial doses comparable to dimethoate; global conventional use ~0.1–0.15 kg a.i./ha per application, typically 1–2 applications per season in regions where it remains registered. Banned from EU olive use under Regulation 2018/783 (outdoor uses), so current global use is concentrated in non-EU producing regions (Tunisia, Morocco, Turkey, California). Value of 0.12 kg/ha represents a global production-weighted average including both applying and non-applying regions.

source.title: Lozano et al. (2021) — Pesticide Residues in Honeybees, Bumblebees and Olive Oil after Applications Against Olive Fruit Fly (PMC/Insects)
source.note: Olive oil — mancozeb kg_ha: Dithiocarbamate fungicide used alongside copper compounds for olive leaf spot (Venturia oleaginea / Colletotrichum gloeosporioides) and as a protectant fungicide. Applied at 0.3–0.5 kg a.i./ha per application in systems where copper alone is insufficient; 1–2 applications per year typical. Note: copper compounds (copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride) are the primary fungicide in olive production globally at 2–3 kg Cu/ha/yr, but copper is an inorganic element not represented in this pesticides list. Mancozeb at 0.5 kg/ha represents secondary synthetic fungicide use in conventional non-organic olive systems.

source.title: Poore & Nemecek (2018) — Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers (Science)
source.note: Canola/rapeseed oil — emissions_per_kg: ~3.69 kg CO2e/kg, cradle-to-retail global weighted average (Poore & Nemecek 2018 'Rapeseed Oil' row, via OWID's food-emissions-supply-chain dataset). Stage breakdown: land-use change 0.20 (small — rapeseed has comparatively little deforestation-linked LUC vs. soy/palm) + farm 2.16 + processing/animal-feed 0.18+0.18 + transport 0.04 + packaging 0.78 + retail 0.24 = 3.69. P&N's methodology allocates co-product impact between rapeseed oil and rapeseed meal by ECONOMIC VALUE, consistent with this repo's soybean-meal allocation (source 270 note in legumes.json). Canola oil captures the large majority of crush value despite being the mass minority: seed is ~40% oil / ~60% meal by mass (source 321, Canola Council of Canada), but oil sells for roughly 3.5-4x meal's price per kg, implying an approximate 70-75% economic-value share to oil. This 3.69 figure already reflects P&N's own allocation, not a mass split.

source.title: Poore & Nemecek (2018) — Reducing food's environmental impacts through producers and consumers (Science)
source.note: Soybean oil — emissions_per_kg: ~6.36 kg CO2e/kg, cradle-to-retail global weighted average (Poore & Nemecek 2018 'Soybean Oil' row, via OWID's food-emissions-supply-chain dataset). Stage breakdown: land-use change 2.87 (large — driven by Brazil-origin deforestation, which dominates the global soy trade) + farm 1.41 + processing/animal-feed 0.29+0.28 + transport 0.04 + packaging 0.79 + retail 0.66 = 6.36. This is P&N's own economically-allocated oil-side figure: their Data S2 soybean-oil row (LUC 3.096 + farm 1.519 = 4.615 per kg oil, farm-gate) is the same figure legumes.json 'soy' (source 270) used to back out soybean MEAL's farm-gate emissions via ~60% economic allocation to meal / ~40% to oil — so this repo's soybean-oil and soybean-meal emissions figures are internally consistent, derived from the same P&N oil-row data with the same ~40/60 economic split.

source.title: USSEC (2025) — Examining U.S. Soy's Carbon Footprint (Mérieux NutriSciences | Blonk, Agri-footprint 6.3)
source.note: Derived US value: USSEC/Blonk Agri-footprint 6.3 reports US whole soybeans at 0.43 kg CO2e/kg (cradle-to-market, incl. LUC+peat; this repo's legumes.json 'soy' source 276). Applying the same ~40% economic-value allocation to oil and the same 18.3% mass extraction rate used for yield_kg_ha: 0.43 x 0.40 / 0.183 = 0.94 kg CO2e/kg oil on a cradle-to-market (farm+crush) basis. Adding the same processing/packaging/retail increment the world figure carries beyond its farm+crush P&N base (6.36 - 4.615 = 1.76) gives an estimated cradle-to-retail US total of ~0.94 + 1.76 = ~2.6 kg CO2e/kg. Notably lower than the world average because US soy is not linked to Brazil-style deforestation LUC. Confidence 2 — multi-step derivation, not a direct US soybean-oil LCA.

name: Palm Oil
land_types_note: Indonesia and Malaysia; a large share of plantations replaced rainforest, and some drained carbon-rich peat swamp.
sentient_harm_explanation: Palm oil has no direct animal-slaughter component (it's a plant food), but new oil-palm plantations are a leading driver of tropical deforestation in Indonesia and Malaysia, destroying rainforest habitat for orangutans, Sumatran tigers, elephants and other wildlife. This repo doesn't model wildlife habitat loss as a separate death count — it's reflected indirectly through this food's land-use figures (yield_kg_ha, which drives the land-use / crop-deforestation score) and its unusually large land-use-change share of emissions_per_kg.

source.title: FAO — Oil Palm (agronomy chapter: FFB yield, oil extraction rate, fertilizer demand)
source.note: Palm oil — yield_kg_ha is crude palm OIL per hectare, not fresh fruit bunches (FFB). Global average FFB yield ~18-19 t/ha/yr at ~20% oil-extraction rate (OER, typical range 17-27%) gives a global-average crude palm oil yield of ~3.5 t/ha/yr — well below the 11-18 t/ha potential of best-managed plantations, reflecting smallholder and aging-plantation drag on the world average. This is far higher per hectare than any other oil crop (olive ~400, canola ~820, soybean ~512), which is why palm has displaced other oils commercially despite its emissions/deforestation profile. Palm KERNEL oil (~0.4-0.6 t/ha, a secondary product of the kernel/shell, not the fruit pulp) is a minor co-product (~10% of CPO by weight) and is not separately modeled here. The US grows no commercial oil palm (only small experimental plantings in Puerto Rico/Hawaii); all US palm oil is imported, primarily from Indonesia and Malaysia, so no separate region:'US' values are given for this food anywhere below — world figures apply.

source.title: Model estimate — needs proper sourcing
source.note: Palm oil — co2_capture_kg_ha_yr: rough estimate. Oil palm is a perennial tree crop with large standing woody biomass, continuous year-round canopy, and high overall biomass productivity, so growing-season carbon capture is estimated well above annual row crops (soybean 1,500) and above olive (7,000). This reflects standing-crop uptake only — it is not a net carbon balance and does not offset the large one-time land-use-change emissions from clearing forest for new plantings, which are captured separately in emissions_per_kg.

source.note: Palm oil — fertilizer_kg_ha: mature oil palm is heavily fertilized (particularly potassium, given high bunch-yield nutrient removal, plus nitrogen and magnesium); ~350 kg/ha/yr combined NPK+Mg is a representative estimate for conventional mature plantations. No single authoritative global-average figure located; confidence 2.
